name: Varun Singh
bio: Pre-training lead at Arcee AI working on end to end pre-training of large language models, with a strong interest in architecture and optimization. Led the pre-training of Arcee's Trinity series of models, ranging from a 6B mixture-of-experts to a 400B mixture-of-experts model.

positions.claim: Synthetic data is the way forward for pre-training, despite the common warning that it causes model collapse.
Web text has fallen from ~85% of GPT-3's training mix to ~15% in MAI Thinking 1, with code and STEM data taking its place.
Post-training-style SFT and agentic data should be pulled back into pre-training so the model learns downstream task shapes from the beginning.
Code is now the dominating data subset in pre-training recipes, whereas GPT-3 had no dedicated code datasets.

MoE expert load imbalance during post-training is a symptom of pre/post-training distribution mismatch, and raising the load-balancing coefficient late in training is an inferior fix compared to better early data mixing.
The pre-training / mid-training / post-training / RL taxonomy is muddy and should be replaced with two paradigms: supervised next-token prediction and RL.
Because RL now dominates the compute budget, supervised learning's purpose is to build useful representations for RL rather than to be the model's main capability source.
A base model only needs exposure to the atomic skills RL will later compose; RL can extrapolate from there if the environment is difficult enough.
Language models are unlikely to follow AlphaGo's trajectory of RL fully overtaking supervised learning, because human language is too broad a distribution to learn from RL alone.
If a new interaction paradigm replaces reasoning and agents, base models should be redesigned as priors for that paradigm rather than as web-text archives.
Long-context and agentic-trace datasets currently reserved for mid-training could be moved into pre-training without harm, yielding more stable representations.
The one-version-for-everyone model was never chosen on merit; it was the only economically viable shape given the cost of producing a correct change.
The cost of producing a correct, scoped code change is collapsing toward zero, and production no longer has to happen in one place before anyone runs the software.
Brittleness in AI-generated systems comes from unmanaged divergence inside a single tangled artifact with no boundaries, not from the code being AI-generated.
A stem-plus-bounded-divergences architecture limits the blast radius of any change to a single user context and makes rollback possible without a deploy.
Developers should be able to declare regions like auth and payments permanently off limits to adaptation, while other regions such as form layout stay adaptable.
Adaptive software lets a horizontal SaaS product serve a much wider set of customer personas without increasing R&D spend.
With no single artifact, identifying what a user is running becomes a graph query over immutable divergences rather than a version number lookup.
The recommendations-only, never-autonomous approach is defensible but is the wrong long-term target; the goal should be earning enough trust that humans choose to step back.
Updates should propagate by merging intent and outcome rather than code, so users converge on shared goals without running the same commit.
Code generation is roughly the easy 80% of the problem; observability, validation, provenance, and coordination are where the durable business value lies.
Existing personalization infrastructure — feature flags, segmentation, A/B testing — is fundamentally limited because segments must be declared in advance.
Measuring whether an adaptation is desirable requires tying it to company-specific goal metrics like retention, churn, or support ticket volume, and correctness testing alone is insufficient.
